extras.description: Primary single credits Bipul Chettri voice/guitars/damphu; Pranai Gurung electric guitars; Aman Singh Rathore drums; Rahul Rai fretless bass; Ganesh Dutta violins/viola; Prince Nepali sarangi; Sonam Tashi backing voice/triangle. Artist tags Nepali and indie folk. Prince own Sarangi Ghar biography confirms Nepali Gandharba sarangi practice and work with Bipul. Complete ten-card single palette and exactly two credited singers. Nepali is a language/cultural independent-music category, not a claim that Indian-born Kalimpong artist lives in Nepal. Selected arranged folk-pop reproduction uses authored recurring verse/refrain and functional-harmony architecture under broad functionalSong; no claim measured source structure or all Nepali indie share it. extras.description: Smithsonian track record credits Hasan Kasa'i on ney alone and identifies a four-minute-eight-second free improvisation in shushtari, within dastgah homayun. Institutional explanation explicitly describes the Iranian interdental blowing technique. The precisely indexed complete track has one ney performer and zero credited singers; no accompaniment is added. An isolated Persian owner avoids the existing ney card nine-segment/seven-hole construction while preserving that old owner unchanged. Authored seven-segment six-hole cane realization and continuous legato follow compatible regional practice; source actual cane species, exact length, base pitch and mouthpiece material were not measured, with base pitch explicitly left unspecified. Existing Persian dastgah tuning framework is a rendering model, not an exact transcription of every intonation. Isfahan reflects positively identified master lineage/community, not an inferred recording address. Authored present-day recording arrangement based on the documented selected performance branch. extras.description: Artist/label release explicitly identifies Nfaly Diakite as the only singer, performing all backing vocals, donso ngoni and keregne across the complete nine-track album, recorded June2020 in Studio Zack, Bamako and released2024. The instrument is described as an eight-string antelope-skin harp. The source presents hunter-praiser songs transmitting Bambara history and philosophical narratives, in a tribute to storyteller/poet Toumani Kone. Three role families, one distinct singer; former BKO collaborators are biographical context, not album performers. Broad Ngoni listening category includes this documented hunter-harp branch; not a claim that harp-lute and spike-lute constructions are identical or that all ngoni music belongs to hunter ritual. extras.description: Artist-owned biography identifies Fotefar as a northern Norwegian regional ensemble and credits Lena Jinnegren voice and pedal organ, Ragnhild Furebotten fiddle, Bendik Lund Haanshus guitar. Their core repertoire explicitly includes northern Norwegian traditional music, Swedish songs and originals. It separately identifies Vise i Vestavind as the three-person concert version developed from a Helge Stangnes poetry tribute, toured in2023 and planned again2024. One named singer and four instrumental/vocal families in this documented trio practice. Northern Norwegian music is the regional category; selected song-and-poetry trio branch is not equivalent to all Norwegian folk or the separate Nordnorsk Ponk category. Preserve Lena pedal organ from the explicit core roster even though some event publicity shortens her role to voice. Earlier2017 album arrangements with Julie Alapnes and additional backing/archive voices are outside this independently documented trio-concert scope; their singer count is not silently applied to the trio. Ballad/poetry ancestry follows the named poet-tribute-derived concert, not a blanket ancestry for all Northern Norwegian music.
